"Solar-powered Coasts, Wind-powered Core"

While looking at this graph, I noticed that states currently using wind power are a part of the mid-region of the US. It's somewhat surprising because these states are less "busy"/populated, and possibly do not emit fossil fuels compared to more populous states. Could the mid-region be less populated, and have excess land for wind turbines and solar panels (excluding solar-powered homes)? The coasts of the US present a different interest for wind power and alternatives for power in general. For example, although they display a higher solar footprint, there do not seem to be many homes/places that utilize solar panels/solar energy. I've always considered San Diego a unique place because there are solar panels on the roofs of almost every home. It's still not enough to produce change. The mid-region of the US is dominating with wind power- but it could be the acts of companies, land availability, and a windy climate, rather than individual efforts by residents.

comments.raw_comment:
The United States transformation into a Green Machine

In this graph I noticed that the places that are optimal for solar and wind power production are different form the places where the majority of the United States's population (and subsequently the places in which the majority of the U.S.'s power needs are located). This means that for green power production to truly be effective we must build a large amount of infrastructure (mainly in the form of long range power lines and transformer stations) to transport the electricity form where it is being generated and where it is needed. This could cause problems for the implementation of clean energy if not addressed. I wonder what the chart for projected green energy production by 2050 across the U.S. would look like rather than the chart for needed power production to reach net zero, and if the charts would look at all alike. I also wonder if a carbon removal system would remove a comparable amount of carbon from the air as building a green power plant that costs the same and then shutting down a carbon emitting power plant that produces a comparable amount of electricity.

I notice that there needs to be extensive growth in both wind and solar in the US in order to meet that goal by 2050. I also noticed that there needs to be much more growth in terms of wind than solar power.

Interestingly Hawaii is not featured in this study. However I believe that Hawaii has committed to a plan to become completely carbon neutral by 2045. This graph does not relate directly to us but it is interesting to note that Hawaii is supposedly at least 5 years ahead of the curve. That being said I must emphasize the “supposedly”, Hawaii is notoriously bad at implementing plans (all my Hawaiian homies know exactly what I’m talking about).

Thanks to all of the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Green Work Makes the Dream Work! How Green America Will Be in the Future!” by The Montessori School of Shreveport, Louisiana; "Catching the Wind and Sun for a Better Future" by Hudson of Portland, Oregon; "Can America Tolerate a Bigger Solar and Wind Farm Footprint?" by Karen of Iowa; "Wind and Solar Power: The Best Things In Life Are ‘Free’" by Joey of New Hampshire; and "The Power of the Sun and Wind Against Climate Change.  Which Will Win?”  by Emma of California.
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Nov. 5 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a Stat Nugget.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that there are two maps on display with different colors pertaining to wind or solar power. The first map shows us what the current situation is for the US having wind and solar power, versus the second map which displays just how much wind and solar power we NEED by 2050. Right from the bat I notice just how much more power we need. The two maps show a very little amount versus a large amount. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder where this map got the statistic that proves how much we need by the year 2050? Is this going off of the skepulations that we are running out of natural gases and such and will be reliant on wind and solar power. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
For me and my community, I know of very few people who use solar power to power their homes, and I know of no one who uses wind power. One cool thing I know about solar power is that a friend of mine has a retractible pool cover which heats the pool using solar power. If by 2050 we will be using lots of solar and wind power, many changes need to be made in the coming years. 
Headline?
"The future of power"

This week’s WGOITG is so timely - we just had a  conversation Monday about this very topic! We discussed the benefits and disadvantages of fossil fuels, and this graph shows the country looking for better ways to get energy. Fossil fuels are non renewable, but wind and solar energy are renewable. 

We noticed: In the 2050 map: there is more orange in the east than west; the center of the country has mainly wind, with solar on the coasts; there will be wind energy off the coasts. Hawaii and Alaska are not included in either map. 

We wonder: How much fossil fuel will we still use in this net zero scenario? Why won’t there be more solar energy? How will wind energy work on the ocean? What will be the side effects of these changes? Why are we still relying so much on fossil fuels? 

The connection to our community:
In north Louisiana, there are not currently any wind or solar sources, and in 2050, Louisiana is not going to get much more than it has now. Does fewer sites in our state mean we will still be using fossil fuels, or will we get our energy from other states? Why doesn’t the 2050 map show more windfarms off our coast? Oil and gas have a strong presence in our state. We wonder how much influence this will have in the next 30 years. 

Some possible headlines: 
“Green-work makes the Dream-work! How green America will be in the future!”
“Our 50 State Plan for 2050”
“Renewable sources of energy and you: How we can work together to fight climate change!"

comments.raw_comment:
Title: "The Strive for Sustainable Energy"

I notice that the places that already have solar and wind energy are the main ones that are aiming to grow by 2050. These are also the more flat areas of the United States, unlike areas such as Washington and Oregon that are more mountainous and have rocky landscapes. What I find interesting is that there is an area around the Rocky Mountains where there is less of a need but in the area around the Appalachian Mountains there is not. I wonder if this is because the Rockies are windier compared to the Appalachians so they already have all of it they need or if there just is no need for it around that area. I also notice that the most concentrated areas are in central and the northeast (around New England) and not in the west which surprises me due to the difference in population in places like Nevada with Las Vegas and California with Los Angeles. One thing I wonder is why there are some areas that are off the map that are shown to need the wind and solar power. Is this for fishing purposes? Or is it for something like powering off-land structures such as oil extracting sites or even lighthouses in those areas? I also wonder what the steps are that the nation is planning on taking to reach these goals and if there is any way that I can take part in helping it become a reality especially as I become older.

I notice that we are nowhere close to the amount of wind and solar energy needed. By 2050 we will have to do a lot of work to get people to start using things by means of solar and wind energy. By 2050 we will need the middle of the country to have much more solar energy. This is the area where we need it the most. We need more solar energy in California, and in the South East. I can tell just by looking at it that we are not even close to achieving our goal, so everyone has to work really hard to get it.

I wonder if it is possible. I really hope it is because if we can't do it we are toast. Especially in places like California and the South East we are nowhere close to achieving our goals for solar energy, and I don't know if we can unless everyone tries. Currently, we have just passed the 50% mark of people believing in global warming, and if we can't get that to 100%, we are going to have some problems on our planet.

This relates to me and my community because in New Hampshire we need much more solar and wind energy. Currently it says that our footprint today is so small that it isn't even on the map. This is really bad because it shows how much we have to do to reach our goal. I think it is possible, but only if people can accept what is going on around them.

comments.raw_comment: This map chart shows where wind and solar power farms are currently located in the U.S. on one map and the number of those farms that we will need in order to have net-zero emission by 2050 on another.   It looks like we need about ten times the number of wind farms we currently have in the next 29 years if we are to meet the net-zero emissions goal.  The 2050 map also has a lot more wind than solar farms. It shows that we will need to expand wind farms into the ocean areas off the coasts of many northeastern states, as well as a some southern and northwestern states.  This may not be very well-received by the people who live there.  Those places are know for their tourism and they might be worried that the wind farms will be ugly and affect whether people want to come to their beaches. I wonder how the Princeton Net-Zero American study determined where to put the new wind and solar farms.  Right now there is only a small amount of land in Iowa where there are wind farms.  The net-zero map would require about 3/4 of Iowa to be covered in wind farms.  Right now the windmills can be in farm fields and don't reduce the amount of land that can be farmed.  But with so many more windmills would Iowa lose farmland?  This could be a problem for the whole U.S. because we grow a lot of feed corn that is used around the country.  A catchy title for the graph would be "Can America Tolerate a Bigger Solar and Wind Farm Footprint?"

However, climate change is a global issue and if a problem can be solved only a large scale in a big country, it's obviously more applicable to a smaller country than vice-versa.
